citations.narrative:
The facility exhibits animals in a manner that does not pose minimal risk of harm to the animals and members of the
public. APHIS Officials reviewed several social media photos that were posted on 1-February-2026, 15-March-2026, 25-
March-2026, and 9-April-2026 of a juvenile bobcat on the shoulders and heads of patrons during public exhibition. In
these photos the bobcat is near the faces or touching face to face with the members of the public during the interaction.
The facility representative viewed the photos and confirmed that the photos were taken at the facility and that the
individuals interacting with the bobcat were members of the public. The representative stated that the facility has already
discontinued public interactions with the bobcat due to its increasing size and strength.
Allowing animals to climb on the heads, necks, and shoulders of the public is not a method of handling with minimal risk to
the public and to the animal. It can lead to zoonotic disease transmission, injury to animals and/or the public if the animal
is surprised or frightened. The licensee must ensure that during public exhibition, any animal must be handled so there is
minimal risk of harm to the animal and to the public, with sufficient distance and/or barriers between the animal and the
general viewing public to assure the safety of animals and the public.
Correct by 14-July-2026.

The facility does not have an adequate method of direct control for non-human primates during periods of physical contact
with the public. The facility currently allows members of the public to enter the lemur enclosure and feed the animals with
a representative present taking photos. APHIS Officials reviewed several social media photos that were posted on 31-
January-2026, 1-February-2026, 3-February-2026, and 21-March-2026 where there is no discernible method of direct
control such as a leash, harness, or representative holding the animals. A video posted on 5-May-2026 shows a member
of the public conducting a commercial where the individual is feeding the lemurs again with no discernable method of
direct control by an experienced handler or trainer. The facility representative viewed the photos and confirmed that the
photos were taken at the facility and that the individuals interacting with the lemurs were members of the public. APHIS
officials inquired how the facility maintains direct control of the lemurs when there are periods of physical contact with the
public. The facility representative stated they do not utilize any sort of leash or harness and do not have a reliable recall
method for these lemurs.
Insufficiently controlled animal encounters can result in injury or stress to the animals or the public. A lack of direct control
of the non-human primates could allow the animals to jump on the shoulders and heads of the patrons exposing them to
zoonotic disease transmission and risk of an accidental injury.
Nonhuman primates used in trained animal acts or in uncaged public exhibits must be under the direct control and
supervision of an experienced handler or trainer at all times when the public is present. Trained nonhuman primates may
be permitted physical contact with the public, as allowed under § 2.131, but only if they are under the direct control and
supervision of an experienced handler or trainer at all times during the contact.
Correct by 14-July-2026
This inspection and exit interview were conducted with the facility representative.
Additional Inspectors:
Mark Sanderbeck, ANIMAL CARE INSPECTOR n
